evidence_notes: Claim: the Face on Mars is a natural landform, stated in sentence one and re-asserted in the close; support is a chronological retelling of the source (Viking 1 shadows, the 1998 MGS image, Garvin's Middle Butte comparison), all drawn from the passage and much of it in the source's own phrasing. org 4 (idea early and held, frame present, but the three source items are interchangeable supports; rung 5 fails); dev 3 (specific source details, but stitched from lightly transformed source phrasing, some unmarked -- patchwriting caps at 3, and the items are listed for the reader to connect); conv 3 (errors accumulate -- shawdowy, scientisits, peole, unclosed quotation -- and the tangled double-'when' body sentence forces a re-read); arg 3 (position clear and committed, but the why is never stated: the essay reports that scientists concluded it, never why sharper images settle the shadow question, and the close circles back).

Claim: the popular vote is the best way to elect a president, stated at the end of the intro; two source quotes (paragraph ten on electors, paragraph thirteen on winner-take-all and swing states), each followed by the writer's own gloss on what it means for a voter. org 4 (idea early and held, frame present, but the 'EC is complicated' and 'EC is unfair' parts could swap without loss); dev 4 (support is specific and quoted, connection stated, but quotes are dropped in alongside the writer's sentences with 'In paragraph thirteen the second sentence states' and several claims -- the opening bias material, the conclusion's benefits -- go unsupported); conv 3 (contreversy, poeple, 'thought them' for taught, inputing; the 'raised with a certain way that their parents might have thought them was correct' sentence needs repair on a re-read); arg 4 (the elector/swing-state reasons are actually reasoned -- you delegate your preference, independents get no chance -- but the counterview is mentioned and answered only by restating commitment, and the conclusion is what the prompt already implies).

Claim: the author of 'The Challenge of Exploring Venus' gives very little insight into why the pursuit is worth it; support is the article's own content (Earth-like density/size, the ocean-and-life hypothesis, a cited quote on Venus as nearest planetary option, the 800-degree heat and metal-liquifying pressure), each followed by a charge that the author does not go into depth. org 4 (idea early and held, frame present, but the two body sub-points swap freely and the closing adds a support rather than landing the argument); dev 4 (specific, cited support and the connection is stated, but the explanations mostly restate the same verdict -- 'gives very little', 'does not go into depth' -- rather than interpret); conv 3 (dense misspellings -- expirenced, inhosbitable, Dispite, crusial, covincing -- plus unpunctuated run-ons; the opening 'one the closes planet to Earth' must be repaired on a re-read); arg 4 (one reason genuinely reasoned: given heat and pressure this extreme, a justification must say what we would get, and the article never does; but the other side is only conceded in passing and the verdict is one the prompt's framing already offers).

Claim: the author supported his idea that studying Venus is worthy, 'shows his enthusiasm', with a three-part preview; support is three cited quote-drops (sulfuric acid clouds, the 'challenging planet' line, the rocky-surface features line) each tagged with a short 'shows...' phrase. org 3 (the curiosity/dangerous-endeavors part is answered with sulfuric acid, which does not bear on it -- the unit starts one job and finishes another, and the one-line close stops rather than closes); dev 3 (quotes are specific but listed, and the tacked-on 'shows the challenge' merely repeats the quote instead of connecting it to the claim; the reader supplies the link); conv 2 (sugestion, curitostity, astronimers, simalaritis, multitued, artical, plus 'When the author's how human curiosity lead to dangerous endeavors is shown in paragraph 3' -- at least twice the reader must guess the intent, not repair it); arg 3 (a position is discernible and committed in the close -- 'his idea has a multitued of support' -- but every reason is a quote plus a restatement; nothing is shown to follow).

Claim: the Facial Action Coding System is valuable in the classroom and should be implemented, stated in sentence one; the reasons offered are that it reads emotion and adjusts the lesson plan, that test results will improve, and that every child deserves an education, plus stretches on texting and laziness and a closing turn to PTSD patients. org 3 (controlling idea stated up front but the texting/laziness parts do not relate to it, there is no closing at all, and the essay ends on a new topic); dev 2 (support is general throughout -- no named case, figure or realized example anywhere; 'most of the students fail' is a vague gesture, and the implementation claim is supported by restating itself); conv 3 (errors accumulate -- eligiable, tecnology, 'the only way that communicate mainly is through texting', 'The reason ... should be implemented ... because' -- and each of those needs a re-read to repair, though meaning stays recoverable); arg 3 (position clear but reasons are asserted: why emotion-reading raises test scores is never said, and consecutive paragraphs restate the position in different words).

Claim: going to Venus is dangerous 'but its worth the try', buried in a run-on opening; support is source facts -- 97% carbon dioxide, 800 degrees Fahrenheit, pressure 90 times Earth's, silicon carbide electronics lasting three weeks -- reported without being turned toward the claim. org 3 (a controlling idea is stated in the essay's own words, but there is no closing, the essay stops on an electronics detail, and the opening paragraph carries danger, courage, NASA, worth-it, oxygen and planetary twinning in one jumbled unit); dev 3 (the figures are specific but purely listed -- the essay never says what any of them shows about whether the trip is worth it); conv 2 (fused sentences throughout, missing capitals, 'there oxygen', 'venus density and size are occasionally bigger' and 'so the heat of any kind of phone or tablet resist the pressure of heat' force the reader to guess rather than repair); arg 2 (the 'worth the try' stance is a fleeting clause inside a run-on and is never taken up again -- the rest is source reporting, so the position is too limited to count as clear and committed).

Claim: the Face on Mars was not made by aliens and only looked like a face because of shadows; support is three source quotes -- the 'Martian mesa ... unusual shadows' line, the skeptics' 'winter in April 98 -- a cloudy time of the year' objection, and the cloudless April 8 2001 photo -- arranged as objection then answer. org 4 (idea first sentence and held, all parts relate, but the frame is thin: the closing repeats what the opening already said and the body has no second part to build on the first); dev 4 (support is specific -- named dates, Malin, direct quotes -- and the connection is stated, but the explanations restate the source narrative rather than interpret it, and the final quote is left hanging); conv 4 (becasue, quotes left without terminal punctuation, a sentence resuming lowercase after a paragraph break -- visible, but nothing has to be repaired to get the meaning); arg 4 (the cloudy-winter objection is stated with content and answered with the summer photo, which passes the reasoning rung, but the conclusion is exactly what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: the author supported the idea that studying Venus is a worthy pursuit very well, because he raises each danger and then converts it into a positive; support is three quotes (Venus once covered with oceans and able to support life; no spacecraft surviving more than a few hours; silicon carbide electronics lasting three weeks), each set inside the writer's own account of the article's move. org 4 (idea early and held, real frame, but the two body paragraphs are parallel problem-then-solution units that could swap without loss); dev 5 (support specific throughout and nearly all of it explained in a way that adds something -- the ocean quote is turned into a claim about Earth's gain, the silicon carbide quote into a claim about technological alternatives -- rather than restated); conv 4 (contriversal, postives, willl, 'far to extreme', 'posses the question', advacements, 'prevented each spacecraft to survive' -- visible slips, but sentences vary and stay under control and nothing needs repair); arg 4 (the author's strategy is genuinely reasoned, not just asserted, and the outweighing principle is named in the close, but the essay never entertains the contrary verdict and reaches only what the prompt's framing already implies).

Claim: more people should try being a Seagoing Cowboy, stated only in the final paragraph; support is specific detail from the article -- baseball and volleyball in the empty animal hold, table-tennis tournaments and fencing, the Acropolis, Venice's water streets, the aunt's farm, being drafted at 18 -- with a few stated connections ('helped him for the hard work ... but it didn't help for the danger of the sea'). org 3 (the persuasive position arrives late, and the games list and the draft anecdote do not bear on the see-the-world-and-help-people idea the opening puts forward); dev 4 (support is specific and the connection is stated for some of it -- the farm, the awareness that stayed with him -- but much is listed and the 'helps for life like school does' claim is bare); conv 2 (wsa, opend, Seagoign, aslo, touranments, wiht, sould, Luck for Luke, plus 'in the empty hold of the animals been housed' and 'he wsa his way to Greece' -- frequent structural breakdowns that leave the reader guessing at least once); arg 3 (the recommendation is committed in the writer's own voice but never reasoned -- why Luke's experience means you should go is only asserted).

Claim: the Face is just a natural landform, stated at the end of the intro; support is three marked and cited source quotes -- the ten-times-sharper 1998 photo, the maximum-resolution 2001 capture, and the 'Martian equivalent of a butte or mesa' line -- retold in the article's chronological order. org 4 (idea early and held with a real frame, but rung 5 fails: the closing only re-lists what the opening said and the ordering is the source's chronology rather than a build the essay makes); dev 4 (support specific and the connection stated -- 'This proves that they found out the Face was not an alien monument' -- but every explanation restates the quote instead of adding to it); conv 4 (dicovered, 'On paragraph seven' three times, 'Using evidences from the texts', 'The Face got looked a second time' -- visible and the quote-frame pattern is flat, but nothing forces a re-read); arg 3 (position clear and held, but why a sharper photograph settles the shadow question is never stated, and the final paragraph restates the opening point by point).
